edition.title: Slow Burn - Saturday 7 November 2026
edition.fact: Edition 33. The foreigners stayed. Saturday 7 November 2026, edition 33. This edition runs 4,501 words. Foreign investors bought another Rs 13,750 crore of Indian stocks on Friday - their fourteenth straight buying session, taking the run since 16 October past Rs 53,000 crore - and the Sensex closed above 81,000 for a seven-session streak into the Diwali weekend. The verdicts on Thursday night's heavyweight prints landed: Mahindra jumped 6.15%, Titan 3.36% with a wall of target upgrades, and Britannia fell 4.2% on its biggest-ever quarterly revenue. On Wall Street, Friday was a rebound, not a recovery: the Nasdaq rose 1.1% but stayed in correction, down 3.4% on the week. Oil recorded its worst week of the war - Brent down more than 16% - on hopes of an Iranian proposal carried by Qatar. Tesla set the Cybertruck's end for mid-2027. The long read is Britannia - the biscuit company with no known founder, fought over by a king who died in jail, and won by the family that still runs it.
edition.intro: The 5-minute lead route is first; sections carry the detail. The long read: a Rs 295 bakery in 1892 Calcutta, the Biscuit King who died in Tihar, the French marriage that ended at an AGM, and the professionals who built a machine that sells in eighty countries - pegged to Friday's record-revenue quarter the market sold down anyway.

blocks.html: Today's long read: The biscuit with no founder - how a nameless 1892 Calcutta bakery became Britannia, passed through seven owners, survived a hostile takeover and a poisonous joint venture, and posted its biggest revenue ever on Friday while its stock fell 4.2%. Read it here.
The sweep: FIIs bought a net Rs 13,750 crore on Friday - a fourteenth straight buying session and Rs 53,154 crore since 16 October; the Sensex rose 2.17% to 81,028.02 and the Nifty reclaimed 25,000.
The verdicts: M&M jumped 6.15% and Titan 3.36% - Nomura raised its Titan target to Rs 6,150 - while Britannia fell 4.20% on its own record-revenue print and Thermax crashed 17.4%.
The overnight rebound: the Nasdaq bounced 1.1% Friday but stayed in correction and lost 3.4% on the week; Microsoft slipped on a report it plans fewer neoclouds.

Oil's worst week: Brent settled at $98.32, down more than 16% on the week - the steepest of the war - on hopes around an Iranian proposal sent via Qatar; Rapidan's Bob McNally still puts 80% odds on fighting resuming.
The Cybertruck's end date: Tesla will wind down production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, per Musk.
The long read: Britannia - the biscuit with no founder.

1. The foreigners stayed. Thursday's record was not a one-day positioning event: foreign institutional investors bought a net Rs 13,750 crore of Indian equities on Friday, their fourteenth consecutive buying session, taking the run since 16 October to Rs 53,154 crore - and Rs 34,584 crore in just the last five sessions (Economic Times, on exchange data). Domestic institutions sold again, continuing the handoff this paper flagged Thursday. The market kept roaring into the Diwali weekend: the Sensex gained 1,718.01 points (2.17%) to close at 81,028.02 and the Nifty added 493.75 points (2.01%) to 25,030.35, reclaiming 25,000 - a seventh straight winning session for the indices (India Today's wrap; stock prices are BSE official closes). India VIX jumped 13.35% - hedging costs rising even into a rally, with Wall Street's Thursday rout still fresh. One count dispute, named: a second data outlet put Friday at a six-session streak; this paper carries the Economic Times' fourteen, from the same exchange data. Editor's takeaway: two days of foreign conviction have now survived a 5.5% Nasdaq rout - the next test is whether the bid holds through Sunday's Muhurat session and Monday's first full day after it.

2. The verdicts land: M&M and Titan up, Britannia down on its own record. Thursday evening's heavyweight prints got their market verdicts on Friday, and they split. Mahindra & Mahindra - whose Rs 5,102 crore standalone profit beat the poll, per the company's release - jumped 6.15% to Rs 3,295.00, closing at its day high. Titan, whose profit more than doubled on a customs-duty one-off, rose 3.36% to Rs 4,994.00 after touching Rs 5,013; Nomura raised its target to Rs 6,150 from Rs 5,425, Jefferies upgraded to Buy with a Rs 6,000 target, and JPMorgan stayed neutral (CNBC TV18's Earnings Central; prices BSE official). ONGC - 47% profit growth and an Rs 8 dividend - added a quieter 0.83% to Rs 232.00. The counter-case was Britannia, which reported midday Friday: consolidated revenue up 16.6% to a record Rs 5,542 crore, operating profit up 8.5% to Rs 943 crore, and the stock fell 4.20% to Rs 4,790.00 (BSE official low Rs 4,715.00; two intraday lows circulating in coverage, Rs 4,828 and Rs 4,749.30, are stale - the official print is lower). The session's casualty was Thermax: profit down 4.2% with a Rs 15 crore impairment, and the stock crashed 17.42% to Rs 2,743.85 (Earnings Central). Editor's takeaway: the flood is still paying for quality of beat, not size of print - Titan's one-off was bought, Britannia's record was sold, and a 4% profit dip cost Thermax nearly a fifth of its market value in a day.

3. Wall Street: a rebound, not a recovery. Friday in New York, the Nasdaq composite rose 1.09% to 24,579.42 - a bounce off Thursday's 5.5% collapse that left the index still in correction and down 3.4% for the week; the S&P 500 added 0.31% to 7,376.86 (week: -2.7%) and the Dow slipped 0.46% to 51,285.73 (week: -0.9%) (Kiplinger's closing report; final closes via Anadolu). Thursday's losers led the bounce: Micron rose 5.1% and Nvidia 2.8%. The tell of the session was Microsoft, down 1.0% on reports it plans to work with fewer neoclouds - the specialized data-center landlords financing the AI buildout; CoreWeave, the biggest of them, rose 6.3% ahead of its earnings next week. Elsewhere in the print season: Airbnb jumped 11.7% on revenue up 19% - its fastest in three years - while DraftKings cratered 21.3%, its worst day since November 2022, after cutting its outlook on prediction-market spending (Kiplinger). Editor's takeaway: one green day inside a correction is arithmetic, not absolution - the Microsoft report is the first sign the capex reappraisal is moving from politics into procurement, and CoreWeave's print is the next hard data point.

4. Oil just had its worst week of the war. Brent settled Friday at $98.32 a barrel, up three cents on the day but down more than 16% on the week; WTI settled at $90.83, down about 13% on the week - the steepest weekly falls since the conflict began (CNBC). The driver is hope, not supply: Iran has sent a nuclear proposal to Washington via Qatar, per a senior Iranian official quoted by Reuters, and the market is pricing a diplomatic breakthrough. The counterweights are named: Rapidan Energy's Bob McNally told CNBC he puts an 80% probability on fighting resuming with both benchmarks back above $100, and Lombard Odier's strategists share the view; McNally frames the stakes bluntly: President Trump is "determined, as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon." The security picture did not improve with the price: Iran reported three additional tanker attacks in Hormuz on Thursday and the UK's maritime agency says attacks are running at a near-record rate. That count conflicts with Thursday's edition, which carried the IRGC's figure of four tankers hitting mines, per BBC, Dawn, Xinhua and Reuters - both counts are named here; the discrepancy is Tehran's own messaging. Editor's takeaway: a 16% weekly fall on a proposal that has not been answered is a lot of diplomacy pre-paid - the tripwires remain the detained tankers, the attack tempo, and Washington's actual reply.

5. Tesla sets the Cybertruck's end date. Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas gigafactory around mid-2027, Elon Musk said in a post on X on Friday, calling it both "the best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and "the end of an era"; the factory space makes room for the Cybercab robotaxi (NBC News, with Reuters). The numbers behind the retreat: US sales of 20,237 trucks last year, down 48% from 38,965 in 2024, per Kelley Blue Book - against Musk's own prediction of 250,000 a year. Deliveries began only in late 2023, four years after an unveiling remembered for metal balls cracking the truck's "shatterproof" windows. Former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer's verdict, quoted by NBC, is the obituary line. Editor's takeaway: the pickup designed to be unkillable lasted about three and a half production years - watch what the same Texas floor space says about how much of Tesla's future is now robotaxis, not cars.

6. Friday's second flood: Hindalco's record, Honasa's best, and the rest. The results torrent continued Friday with its own winners and wounds. Hindalco posted its strongest quarter ever: consolidated profit more than doubled to Rs 5,132 crore from Rs 2,266 crore, revenue rose 42.7% to Rs 35,369 crore, aluminium EBITDA jumped 53.4% to Rs 7,338 crore, copper EBITDA hit a record Rs 1,673 crore (up 164%), and Novelis - its US arm - delivered adjusted EBITDA of $508 million, up 20.4%, with the Oswego plant back to normal and Bay Minette commissioning; the stock recovered from a 5% intraday fall to close at its day high, Rs 957.70, up 1.88%. Honasa, the Mamaearth parent, reported revenue up 35.9% to Rs 731 crore - its highest since listing - with profit up 87.2% to Rs 73 crore; the stock fell 3.31% anyway. Mphasis guided FY27 growth at the upper end of its range and closed up 0.55% after rising 8% intraday; Siemens grew orders 37.8% and closed up 3.85%; Voltas kept its No. 1 air-conditioner spot with profit up 53.4% and still fell 2.43%; Gland Pharma's profit rose 58.2%; Blue Dart's rose 28.4%; Ratnamani's fell 25% (Earnings Central, all prints; all prices BSE official). Editor's takeaway: read Honasa beside Thursday's Nykaa - another consumer listing, another near-double profit, another red close; the market keeps pricing durability, not growth.

Friday 6 November, Indian close: Sensex 81,028.02 (+1,718.01, +2.17%); Nifty 25,030.35 (+493.75, +2.01%) - a seventh straight winning session, closing above 25,000 into the Diwali weekend. India VIX jumped 13.35% (India Today; index closes per the exchange wrap).

Repro, day three: the week's new equity listing slipped 0.95% to Rs 313.10 on Friday (BSE official). The EAAA bond (10.8%, BSE symbol 108EAAAL27): Friday's print is not in the equity cash-market data this desk uses, and this paper does not guess at debt-segment numbers - the line returns when a verified close is available; Thursday's close was 109,619, a 9.6% premium to face value. In the pipeline: Anthropic's amended S-1, with its third-quarter financials on the public record, remains the filing to read (carried from edition 32).

blocks.html: In New York (Friday finals): S&P 500 7,376.86 (+0.31%, week -2.7%); Dow 51,285.73 (-0.46%, week -0.9%); Nasdaq 24,579.42 (+1.09%, week -3.4%, still in correction); the VIX fell 9.23% to 25.58. Micron +5.1%, Nvidia +2.8%, Microsoft -1.0%, CoreWeave +6.3%, Airbnb +11.7%, DraftKings -21.3% (Kiplinger; Anadolu, final closes).
Oil: Brent settled $98.32 (+$0.03; week -16%+); WTI $90.83 (+$0.31; week about -13%) - both benchmarks' worst week of the conflict, on hopes around Iran's proposal via Qatar (CNBC).

Bosch doubled up on Friday: its board approved a 3:1 bonus issue - three new Rs 2 shares for every one held, about 442.4 million shares out of retained earnings - alongside a 1:5 stock split sub-dividing each Rs 10 share into five Rs 2 shares, both subject to shareholder approval by postal ballot, with completion targeted within two months and the record date still to be fixed (the company's own BSE filing, 6 November). ONGC's Rs 8 interim dividend was declared with Thursday's print. Infosys's Rs 26 dividend pays out on Wednesday 11 November.

The ledger of the streak. Since 16 October, foreign investors have bought a net Rs 53,154 crore of Indian equities across fourteen straight sessions; the last five alone account for Rs 34,584 crore - Thursday's record Rs 14,975 crore plus Friday's Rs 13,750 crore (Economic Times, on exchange data). The other side of the tape did not blink: domestic institutions sold again on Friday, extending the handoff pattern - foreigners buying what locals sell. The arithmetic that matters: the last two sessions supplied 54% of the entire streak's buying, and the last five 65% - which means the average day in this run is far smaller than the headline, and that the run's continuation, not its size, is the signal. Going into the holiday weekend the scoreboard reads: Sensex 81,028, up 2.17% on the day and seven sessions straight; a Rs 53,154 crore foreign bid; and a Nasdaq correction waiting across the weekend.

Honasa's best quarter as a listed company - and the market sold it. The Mamaearth parent's revenue rose 35.9% to Rs 731 crore, its highest since listing, with profit up 87.2% to Rs 73 crore and its focus categories growing 40%; the stock closed down 3.31% at Rs 465.70 (BSE; Earnings Central). It is Thursday's Nykaa verdict in miniature: triple-digit-adjacent profit growth, red close. Two sessions, two consumer listings, one message - the multiple still does the talking. Lenskart, day after the 52-week high: the eyewear retailer added 0.88% to Rs 724.70, holding the bulk of its post-results move - the first verdict keeps standing. The frame: this week's consumer-internet scorecard reads one pass (Lenskart), two sells (Nykaa, Honasa) - growth durability is being priced, not growth.

Google cut the price of generated video while the market questioned the buildout. Google released Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash on Thursday: native 15-second video generation, up from 10; 30% cheaper at $0.07 per second for 720p; multi-turn conversational editing that swaps products, backgrounds, lighting or aspect ratio without regenerating the clip; and reference adherence that holds a person's identity and garments across shots - generally available on the Gemini API and Google Cloud (Google's announcement). The same week, the demand side of the AI trade wobbled: Thursday's correction was still fresh when Microsoft slipped 1% Friday on reports it plans to work with fewer neoclouds - the specialized landlords whose borrowing underpins the data-center buildout (Kiplinger). CoreWeave reports next week - the first neocloud print since the correction began. The counter-file stands: Anthropic's amended S-1 keeps the cost side of the frontier auditable (carried from edition 32). Editor's takeaway: the model layer is getting cheaper and better on schedule; the market is now auditing the landlords - two different clocks, and next week's CoreWeave print is where they meet.

The most consequential line in Google's Omni 1.2 release is not the resolution or the price; it is "multi-turn conversational editing." Until now, changing one thing in an AI-generated video meant regenerating the whole clip - the video equivalent of rewriting a program from scratch to fix one line. The new model keeps the clip and lets you talk it through revisions: swap the product, change the lighting, flip the aspect ratio, and the rest holds still. Anyone who has built software by conversation will recognize the shift instantly - it is the difference between a generator and an editor. The practical rule this desk takes from it: when evaluating any AI creative tool, ask whether it remembers. A tool that preserves your work across instructions is a workflow; a tool that starts over is a slot machine. Video just crossed from the second kind to the first.

If you plan to trade in tomorrow's Muhurat session - and lakhs of families do, as a shagun for Samvat 2083 - decide the token amount tonight, before the one-hour window opens at 2:20 PM. The session runs just 2:20 to 3:30 PM on Sunday, with thin volumes by design; it is a ceremony with a settlement slip, not a trading opportunity. Buy the share you intend to keep, in the amount you would gift, and log off. The first real session of the new year is Monday, and it will have plenty to say.

Once a year, on Diwali, India's exchanges open for a single symbolic hour. Muhurat trading marks the start of the new Hindu financial year - Samvat 2083 begins tomorrow - and BSE, NSE and MCX all run the special session: this year on Sunday 8 November, with a pre-open from 2:05 PM and continuous trading from 2:20 to 3:30 PM (Economic Times' session guide, from the exchange circulars). The tradition is a shagun - an auspicious first transaction - so volumes run light and many participants buy a token share and hold it. What newcomers miss is that the trades are entirely real: they settle like any other day's, with money and shares changing hands on the normal cycle. The session moves no markets by design; what it does is keep a ritual the BSE has run since 1957 wired into the same order books that processed Rs 13,750 crore of foreign buying on Friday. The ritual is the market's, and it survives every regime change - ask Britannia, which has outlived all of them since 1892.

groups.heading: Term of the day: commodity upcycle

blocks.html: An upcycle is the stretch of a commodity's price cycle when demand outruns supply and margins expand for the companies that dig, refine or fabricate it - the mirror image of the downcycle, when the same companies' fixed costs eat their profits. Hindalco's quarter is the textbook entry: aluminium EBITDA up 53.4% and copper EBITDA up 164% in one quarter is not something a management team can manufacture - it is the metal prices doing the lifting, with the company's plants back at normal catching it (Oswego recovered, Bay Minette commissioning). The word matters because cycles end: the same leverage that doubles profit on the way up halves it on the way down. When you read a record commodity quarter, the record is the cycle's, not the company's - the company owns only how much of the upcycle it converted into capacity, and how little debt it carried into the turn.

The desk's rule: every published setup stays on the board until it completes (target hit) or fails (stop hit). Per-share prices on every line; the Rs 1,500 price cap screens what qualifies as a setup. Ledger: Slow Burn swing research, 24 Oct.

blocks.html: The HCLTech line resolves and stays in the ledger: filled 28 October at the worst fill of Rs 1,378.00, target Rs 1,466.80 taken out at Friday's high of Rs 1,468.00 - gross +6.44%, net +6.14% after the 0.3% cost convention, in seven sessions. The stop at Rs 1,346.90 never traded. Kotak (Rs 480.00) held above its Rs 437.55 trigger for a tenth session - still a candidate, not a setup. JSW Steel (Rs 1,359.00) closed at its day high, extended well beyond the reclaimed zone; the published R:R screen still fails it, which is why it stays a watchlist line. ONGC (Rs 232.00) spent a fourth session above 228 inside its Rs 218.50-238.75 coil - and now carries an Rs 8 interim dividend and a 47% consolidated profit print into the weekend, with crude down 16% on the week against it; the coil decides. Infosys (Rs 1,180.65) closed back inside the Rs 1,175 trigger zone ahead of Wednesday's Rs 26 payout. New candidate, watchlist only: Hindalco (Rs 957.70) - momentum (closed at the day high after a 5% intraday shakeout), heavy results-day volume, the strongest quarter in its history as catalyst, and an aluminium-copper upcycle behind it; it fails nothing but proves nothing yet - no entry zone until levels are verified against a longer price history, so it enters as a watchlist line, not a setup. Voltas was screened and rejected: it fell 2.43% on its own beat - the momentum factor fails today. Tech Mahindra stays shelved above the Rs 1,500 cap.

items.detail: Unknowable from daily data: conservative scoring assumes the worst fill, then the stop.

items.title: Resolutions stay on record
items.detail: A setup leaves the board only when its target or stop resolves it; winners and losers both stay in the ledger.

blocks.html: Three conditions, in the order they resolve. First, the streak's holiday test: fourteen sessions and Rs 53,154 crore of foreign buying now meet a one-hour Muhurat session on Sunday and a full Monday after it - whether the bid keeps arriving in size, or shrinks back to the run's average day, tells you whether Thursday and Friday were conviction or crowding. Second, the proposal in Doha's hands: a 16% weekly fall in Brent pre-paid a diplomatic answer that has not been given - what matters is the proposal's actual contents, Washington's reply, and whether the tanker-attack tempo (near-record, per the UK agency) lets the talks breathe. Third, the landlords' audit: Microsoft's reported step back from neoclouds and CoreWeave's earnings next week are the first procurement-level test of the AI buildout since Thursday's correction - the numbers to watch are contracted capacity and capex guidance, not the share prices. This desk does not predict the answers; it watches these conditions.

The FII streak. Cause chain: foreign investors sold Indian equities through most of 2026; since 16 October they have bought fourteen sessions straight - Rs 53,154 crore - with the last two days alone supplying Rs 28,725 crore; domestic funds have sold into the bid throughout. Watch next: the provisional flow prints from the Muhurat session and from Monday - whether the bid holds in size. Proven wrong if: the daily foreign number flips negative and stays there while the indices are still near the week's highs.

The Hormuz reply chain. Cause chain: Iran's seven conditions; a US reply Tehran called "not convincing"; then, this week, an Iranian nuclear proposal carried to Washington by Qatar - and oil's worst week of the war on the hope of it; against that, three further tanker attacks Thursday per Tehran (four, per the IRGC's count carried in Thursday's edition) at a near-record tempo per the UK maritime agency, and two vessels still detained. Watch next: the proposal's contents, Washington's answer, UKMTO incident confirmations. Proven wrong if: a signed agreement lands while tankers are still being attacked and detained.

The AI buildout's audit. Cause chain: Tuesday's election installed leadership hostile to data-center expansion; Thursday's 5.5% Nasdaq rout priced the political risk; Friday brought the first corporate echo - reports that Microsoft plans fewer neocloud partners; CoreWeave, the largest of them, reports next week. Watch next: CoreWeave's contracted-capacity and capex lines, and any Microsoft confirmation. Proven wrong if: hyperscaler capex guidance rises through the correction and the neocloud order books keep lengthening.

items: Sources read for this edition: Economic Times on the FII flows and the streak count; India Today on the Indian close; CNBC TV18’s Earnings Central for every Friday print (Titan broker targets, ONGC, M&M, Hindalco, Honasa, Mphasis, Siemens, Voltas, Gland, Blue Dart, Ratnamani, Thermax, Britannia); Kiplinger’s closing report and Anadolu’s final-close wire for the US finals; CNBC for the oil settles, the Qatar proposal and the McNally view; NBC News with Reuters on the Cybertruck wind-down; Google’s own blog for Omni 1.2 Flash; Bosch’s own BSE filing for the split and bonus; Economic Times’ Muhurat guide for the session times; BSE’s official bhavcopy for every Indian stock price.

Corrections discipline: the FII streak count is carried at fourteen sessions per Economic Times - a second outlet’s six-session count is named in story 1 as a conflict, not merged. Thursday’s tanker count (four, per the IRGC via BBC, Dawn, Xinhua and Reuters) conflicts with CNBC’s Friday report of three additional attacks - both are named in story 4; the UK maritime agency’s near-record tempo line is source-neutral. Britannia’s intraday low is the BSE official Rs 4,715.00 - two higher figures circulating in coverage are stale and named as such in story 2. The EAAA bond has no verified Friday close and says so rather than guessing. Titan, ONGC and M&M reported after Thursday’s close, so Friday’s moves are their verdicts; Britannia reported midday Friday and its fall is a same-day reaction. Anything later than about 6:15 AM IST is deliberately not in this edition.
